7:Weighting judges by their reported confidence is often described as the optimal way to combine binary judgments, but the rule is only conditionally optimal: correlated errors change the optimal weights, miscalibrated competence inputs degrade them, and estimated weights routinely lose to the simple average. We ask the finite-sample question an aggregator can act on: given the number of judges, the confidence–accuracy slope, and the within-item error correlation, when does confidence weighting (CW) lose to equal weighting (EW), and is partial shrinking better than either? We derive the gap, map its boundary in a preregistered simulation, and estimate where 76 datasets from the Confidence Database (1,641,000 trials) sit. The simulation has a clear boundary: CW helps only when confidence is well calibrated, and overconfidence reverses the graded effect. In the data, the decision advantage of CW is negligible (+0.004, 95% CI [0.0003, 0.0083], non-positive in 64% of datasets) and CW worsens the leave-one-judge-out estimate of a judge's correctness in 91% of datasets. Contrary to the account, the harm does not vary with the calibration slope or the error correlation, and the calibrated simulation does not reproduce the data (36% agreement with the decision gap, against a 79% baseline for the graded measure). Confidence weighting is not a safe default, the standard overconfidence account does not explain why, and partial shrinking towards equal weighting is often better.
13:Combining the judgments of several people usually beats asking one. The advantage comes from cancelling idiosyncratic error: if judges are on average better than chance and wrong for different reasons, the simple majority grows more accurate as judges are added (Condorcet, 1785/1994). This result, and the conditions under which it holds (Berend & Paroush, 1998), underpins practical advice to poll, average, or vote rather than to defer to a single expert.
17:Three literatures make the optimality conditional in ways worth stating plainly. First, committee theory shows that the optimal weights depend on the structure of shared error. When voters' judgments are correlated, equal or competence-proportional weighting is not generally optimal (Shapley & Grofman, 1984; Ladha, 1995; Kaniovski, 2010), and additional judges stop helping once their errors move together (Hogarth, 1978; Einhorn et al., 1977). Second, the forecast-combination literature shows that estimated optimal weights routinely fail to beat the simple average, because estimating many weights from few observations adds variance (Smith & Wallis, 2009; Claeskens et al., 2016). Huang, Broomell and Golman (2024) formalise this as a test of whether weighting "reliably improves collective accuracy or just adds noise". Third, when the weights come from a distorted competence signal rather than true competence, the optimal rule degrades (Baharad & Ben-Yashar, 2009). Reported confidence is exactly such a signal, and it is only weakly related to accuracy: pooling 145 datasets, Jin, Verhaeghen and Rahnev (2022) found a positive but modest confidence–accuracy correlation. Empirically, confidence-weighted majority voting can beat unweighted majority voting (Saha Roy et al., 2021; Meyen et al., 2021), and confidence-based rules can make crowds more efficient (Berger et al., 2025), but people themselves weight votes more equally than the optimal confidence rule prescribes (Meyen et al., 2021).
23:This is a Theory Article with an empirical test. We do not claim that confidence weighting can hurt, that correlated error changes optimal weights, or that confidence-weighted voting sometimes beats majority: those are established (Baharad & Ben-Yashar, 2009; Huang et al., 2024; Meyen et al., 2021; Shapley & Grofman, 1984). The contributions are the psychometric parametrisation of the gap, the simulated boundary, the estimated base rate of the harmful region, and a negative result: the simple account does not reproduce the data. Our preregistration, including the analysis plan and the criteria for each outcome, was committed before the outcome variables were analysed; it and every deviation are in the project repository.
47:with $\lambda=0$ reproducing EW and $\lambda=1$ reproducing CW. If the weighting gain and the variance cost trade off, the accuracy-optimal $\lambda^\star$ will often lie strictly between the two, and shrinking towards equal weights is better than either extreme. Whether an interior optimum exists, and where, is a question for the simulation.
64:![**Figure 2.** Simulated boundary surface (gamma = 0.3, omega = 0.05). Colour is the effect of confidence weighting as a function of overconfidence phi and shared error tau. (a) Leave-one-judge-out Brier improvement: positive only for well-calibrated confidence. (b) Sign-accuracy gap: positive for well-calibrated confidence and turning negative at high overconfidence.](analysis/output/figures/fig2_boundary.png)
65: The gap does not increase monotonically with group size as the finite-sample reading predicts: 289 of 1,080 steps exceed the Monte-Carlo tolerance in the decreasing direction, so H2 is not supported and the relation is non-monotone in a substantial minority of cells.
69:An interior optimum is the rule rather than the exception. In 119 of the 120 cells the accuracy-optimal shrinkage $\lambda^\star$ lies strictly between 0 and 1 for at least one group size (Figure 3), so partial shrinking beats both pure rules almost everywhere. The optimal weight on confidence falls as overconfidence rises, reaching zero when confidence is uninformative.
71:![**Figure 3.** Accuracy-optimal shrinkage lambda* between equal weighting (0) and confidence weighting (1) against group size, for three levels of overconfidence. An interior optimum is the rule across the grid.](analysis/output/figures/fig4_lambda.png)
95:The predicted moderation does not appear. Regressing the LOO-Brier improvement on the calibration slope and the within-item error correlation, neither coefficient is distinguishable from zero (calibration slope −0.0003, SE 0.0009; error correlation −0.00001, SE 0.0004). The same holds for the sign-accuracy gap (calibration slope +0.015, SE 0.014; error correlation +0.010, SE 0.007). H5, which predicted that flatter calibration and higher error correlation would make CW worse, is not supported on either measure: the point estimates are near zero and, for the sign measure, in the opposite direction from the prediction.
103:Confidence weighting does not reliably improve crowd judgment in real data, and the standard explanation of why it might not is not supported either. Across 76 datasets and 1.6 million trials, weighting judges by their confidence gave a decision gain of +0.004, non-positive in about two of three datasets, and degraded the leave-one-judge-out estimate of a judge's correctness in 91% of datasets. The simulation shows that a boundary exists: confidence weighting helps both the decision and the graded estimate only when confidence is well calibrated, and overconfidence reverses the graded effect. But the data do not follow the predicted moderation, and the calibrated model does not reproduce the observed signs.
107:What, then, should an aggregator do? The safest reading of these results is that confidence weighting should not be a default. Its typical decision benefit is under half a percentage point of accuracy, it is absent or negative in a majority of datasets, and it makes the graded estimate slightly worse in almost all of them. If confidence weighting is used at all, it should be justified on a calibration set where the analyst can check whether the confidence–accuracy slope is steep enough to matter, and it should be shrunk towards equal weighting, because an interior optimum was the rule in the simulation. The classical argument for weighting remains valid in the regime it was derived for, well-calibrated and largely independent judges, but that regime appears to be the exception rather than the norm in the corpora we can observe.
109:Several limitations bound these conclusions. The empirical leg reuses a corpus not designed for crowd aggregation. Items are condition cells rather than matched physical stimuli, so the analysis measures how confidence reweighting changes the crowd's estimate of a shared condition, not a controlled group decision, and the leave-one-judge-out measure predicts a held-out judge's correctness rather than the item's truth. The datasets differ in task, scale, and confidence format, and we pool them only at the level of summary estimates; the meta-analytic summary is an unweighted mean across datasets, not a random-effects model. The model-reproduction test matches on only two inputs, so its failure could reflect a crude mapping as well as model misspecification, though the size of the miss is too large to dismiss. The simulation itself is a particular generative model, and its failure to fit is a result about that model, not evidence that no account of confidence weighting could work. Finally, the graded estimand was added after the preregistered sign estimand proved ceiling-bound, so it is not confirmatory in the strict sense; the preregistered result is reported throughout and points the same way.
111:The findings point to specific next steps. A designed crowd experiment that holds stimuli fixed across judges could test the graded prediction directly at the group sizes where the theory says the sign turns, and could measure the confidence–accuracy slope on a calibration set before the aggregation decision. A better mechanism than simple overconfidence is needed to explain why confidence weighting fails so consistently; candidates include confidence that tracks item familiarity rather than correctness, and shared information that makes the most confident judges the most correlated ones. And the shrinkage rule deserves evaluation on real crowds, since its value rests on the interior optimum that the simulation found but the data cannot yet confirm.
131:Baharad, E., & Ben-Yashar, R. (2009). The robustness of the optimal weighted majority rule to probability distortion. *Public Choice*, 139(1–2), 53–59. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11127-008-9378-7
143:Condorcet, N. de. (1994). *Essai sur l'application de l'analyse à la probabilité des décisions rendues à la pluralité des voix* [Essay on the application of analysis to the probability of majority decisions]. Imprimerie Royale. (Original work published 1785)
147:Grofman, B. (1978). Judgmental competence of individuals and groups in a dichotomous choice situation: Is a majority of heads better than one? *The Journal of Mathematical Sociology*, 6(1), 47–60. https://doi.org/10.1080/0022250X.1978.9989880
159:Ladha, K. K. (1995). Information pooling through majority-rule voting: Condorcet's jury theorem with correlated votes. *Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization*, 26(3), 353–372. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(94)00068-P
165:Meyen, S., Sigg, D. M. B., von Luxburg, U., & Franz, V. H. (2021). Group decisions based on confidence weighted majority voting. *Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications*, 6(1), 22. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41235-021-00279-0

65: The gap does not increase monotonically with group size as the finite-sample reading predicts: 289 of 1,080 steps exceed the Monte-Carlo tolerance in the decreasing direction, so H2 is not supported and the relation is non-monotone in a substantial minority of cells.
69:An interior optimum is the rule rather than the exception. In 119 of the 120 cells the accuracy-optimal shrinkage $\lambda^\star$ lies strictly between 0 and 1 for at least one group size (Figure 3), so partial shrinking beats both pure rules almost everywhere. The optimal weight on confidence falls as overconfidence rises, reaching zero when confidence is uninformative.

95:The predicted moderation does not appear. Regressing the LOO-Brier improvement on the calibration slope and the within-item error correlation, neither coefficient is distinguishable from zero (calibration slope −0.0003, SE 0.0009; error correlation −0.00001, SE 0.0004). The same holds for the sign-accuracy gap (calibration slope +0.015, SE 0.014; error correlation +0.010, SE 0.007). H5, which predicted that flatter calibration and higher error correlation would make CW worse, is not supported on either measure: the point estimates are near zero and, for the sign measure, in the opposite direction from the prediction.
103:Confidence weighting does not reliably improve crowd judgment in real data, and the standard explanation of why it might not is not supported either. Across 76 datasets and 1.6 million trials, weighting judges by their confidence gave a decision gain of +0.004, non-positive in about two of three datasets, and degraded the leave-one-judge-out estimate of a judge's correctness in 91% of datasets. The simulation shows that a boundary exists: confidence weighting helps both the decision and the graded estimate only when confidence is well calibrated, and overconfidence reverses the graded effect. But the data do not follow the predicted moderation, and the calibrated model does not reproduce the observed signs.
107:What, then, should an aggregator do? The safest reading of these results is that confidence weighting should not be a default. If confidence weighting is used at all, it should be justified on a calibration set where the analyst can check whether the confidence–accuracy slope is steep enough to matter, and it should be shrunk towards equal weighting, because an interior optimum was the rule in the simulation. The classical argument for weighting remains valid in the regime it was derived for, well-calibrated and largely independent judges, but that regime appears to be the exception rather than the norm in the corpora we can observe.
109:Several limitations bound these conclusions. The empirical leg reuses a corpus not designed for crowd aggregation. The simulation itself is a particular generative model, and its failure to fit is a result about that model, not evidence that no account of confidence weighting could work. Finally, the graded estimand was added after the preregistered sign estimand proved ceiling-bound, so it is not confirmatory in the strict sense; the preregistered result is reported throughout and points the same way.
111:The findings point to specific next steps. A better mechanism than simple overconfidence is needed to explain why confidence weighting fails so consistently; candidates include confidence that tracks item familiarity rather than correctness, and shared information that makes the most confident judges the most correlated ones. And the shrinkage rule deserves evaluation on real crowds, since its value rests on the interior optimum that the simulation found but the data cannot yet confirm.

## Answer

**Seven of the eight earlier findings are addressed in the code or reporting.** The eighth, the preregistered random-effects meta-analysis, remains an explicit deviation: the analysis reports an unweighted dataset mean with a bootstrap CI. The revised code samples distinct judges, uses stable CRC32 seeds, computes the ICC on judge–item rows, fits the ridge logistic slope, and compares Brier results at \(m=7\). The [deviation log](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper4/deviations.md:13) acknowledges that Brier predicts a held-out judge’s correctness and that its mean points opposite to the sign-accuracy result. [H6](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper4/analysis/scripts/h6.py:38) uses the preregistered sign test for its support decision: 28/76 (37%), so **H6 is rejected**. The H5 coefficients also support **H5 not supported**; its preregistered prediction was a *positive* calibration-slope coefficient and a *negative* error-correlation coefficient.

**Ranked remaining issues**

1. **Major — new \(m=4\) simulation error.** [simulate.py](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper4/analysis/scripts/simulate.py:107) counts every equal-weight tie as incorrect (`ew > 0`), while confidence weighting usually breaks it. In the saved results, mean EW accuracy falls from 0.753 at \(m=3\) to 0.651 at \(m=4\), then rises to 0.777 at \(m=5\). This creates a mean CW advantage of **+0.107 at \(m=4\)** and contributes 120 of the reported 289 H2 decreases. Removing \(m=4\) from the *saved-output comparison* changes the sign of 41/120 simulated cell means. The published H6 mapping uses those affected means; its 37% agreement needs recalculation after a tie rule is specified. Other H2 decreases and interior optima remain in the saved results without \(m=4\), so this does not by itself reverse H2 or H3.
2. **Major — H6 compares different group-size averages.** [h6.py](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper4/analysis/scripts/h6.py:39) matches each dataset’s average over its eligible empirical sizes to a simulation average over all ten sizes, including \(m=4\). This compounds the tie error and makes the headline H6 result a comparison of different quantities.
3. **Minor — manuscript and log still contradict the outputs.** The [limitations paragraph](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper4/manuscript/manuscript.md:109) says the preregistered sign result and added Brier result “point the same way”; their reported means are **+0.0036** and **−0.0006**. The [log](~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper4/deviations.md:19) correctly says they point in opposite directions, but incorrectly says the manuscript does too. The abstract reports 36% H6 agreement; 28/76 rounds to 37%.
4. **Minor — some interpretation exceeds the evidence.** Claims that partial shrinkage “beats both pure rules almost everywhere” rely on choosing \(\lambda\) on the same simulated items used to score it. The recommendation to shrink in real crowds is stronger than the empirical analysis, which did not test shrinkage there. “Only when confidence is well calibrated” is also too absolute for the saved simulation cells.

The headline labels **H1 supported, H2 not supported, H3 supported, H5 not supported, H6 rejected** are stated, but the manuscript is **not yet internally consistent**, and its simulation-based H2, H3, and H6 numbers should be treated as provisional until the \(m=4\) tie handling is corrected. This was a read-only audit; I did not rerun the pipeline.
